ATTEMPT RECORD from the Codex campaign (author-checked by that worker only). Method: Explicit model calculation, comparison identities and remaining hypothesis obstruction Result: Continuous state alone cannot guarantee1/N weak accuracy for arbitrary observables. If X_i are iid standard normal and their empirical mean is M_N, then E|M_N|=sqrt(2/(pi*N)), whereas the limiting observable is0. The nonsmooth absolute value loses a power of sqrtN. In contrast, a twice differentiable test has its centered first Taylor term vanish and its expected second term of order1/N under a covariance bound. This locates the regularity input a weak-error proof needs. Check: The Gaussian example is exact because M_N has variance1/N. In the queue model, the observable mean workload is linear, but the routing mechanism and the empty-workload boundary create nonsmooth dynamics; smoothness of the observable does not automatically make its Poisson solution smooth. Obstruction: One needs uniform stationary moment bounds, quantitative propagation of chaos and a sufficiently regular Poisson equation or semigroup derivative estimate for the unbounded workload state. The source simulations and the discrete-state refined theorem do not provide those estimates. No matching general continuous-workload proof is supplied.

Load-bearing hypotheses: the periodization $Pf(x)=\sum_nf(x+n)$ must be continuous at the point where the identity is evaluated, and its Fourier series must converge there (absolute summability of $(\hat f(k))_k$ is the usual sufficient condition). For a general $f\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ all that is true is $\widehat{Pf}(k)=\hat f(k)$, i.e. Poisson summation as an identity of Fourier series of an $L^1(\mathbb T)$ function - which says nothing pointwise. Concrete failure: $f=\mathbf 1_{[0,1]}$ (with $f(0)=f(1)=1$). Then $\sum_nf(n)=f(0)+f(1)=2$, while $\hat f(0)=1$ and $\hat f(k)=\int_0^1e^{-2\pi ikx}dx=0$ for $k\ne0$, so $\sum_k\hat f(k)=1\ne2$. The periodization equals $1$ off $\mathbb Z$ and $2$ on $\mathbb Z$: it is discontinuous exactly where the identity is being evaluated, and the Fourier series converges to the midpoint $1$. Redefining $f(0)=f(1)=1/2$ restores the identity. Second trap: pure decay of $f$ is not enough - one needs decay (or summability) on the transform side as well, since the right-hand series must converge; $f$ continuous and integrable with $\hat f$ merely tending to zero gives no pointwise statement. When quoting a rate, the clean hypothesis is $|f(x)|\le C(1+|x|)^{-1-\delta}$ and $|\hat f(\xi)|\le C(1+|\xi|)^{-1-\delta}$ with $f$ continuous, or simply $f\in\mathcal S$.
f integrable on R
the pointwise identity is claimed at a specific point (typically x = 0)
rows.title: Pitfall: Poisson Summation Needs Regularity, Not Just Integrability

rows.body: Let F be in D^{1,2} and let phi be a real continuous function such that phi(F) is in L^2(Omega) and phi(F + D^N F) is in L^2([0,T] x R_0 x Omega). Then phi(F) is in D^{1,2}, D^(1)_t phi(F) = phi'(F) D^(1)_t F and D^(2)_{t,z} phi(F) = phi(F + D^(2)_{t,z} F) - phi(F). Consequently, if G = g(X_{t_1}, ..., X_{t_n}) is in D^(2) for a Lipschitz function g on R^n and (t, z) -> g(X_{t_1} + D^(2)_{t,z} X_{t_1}, ..., X_{t_n} + D^(2)_{t,z} X_{t_n}) - g(X_{t_1}, ..., X_{t_n}) is in L^2([0,T] x R_0 x Omega), then D^(2)_{t,z} G = g(X_{t_1} + D^(2)_{t,z} X_{t_1}, ..., X_{t_n} + D^(2)_{t,z} X_{t_n}) - g(X_{t_1}, ..., X_{t_n}).

Let $\mu$ be a finite positive measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with Stieltjes transform $m(z) = \int \frac{d\mu(t)}{t - z}$, defined and analytic for $\operatorname{Im} z > 0$, with $\operatorname{Im} m(z) > 0$ there. Then for every $a < b$ that are continuity points of $\mu$, $\mu((a, b]) = \lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} \frac{1}{\pi}\int_a^b \operatorname{Im} m(x + i\eta)\,dx$, and if $\mu$ has a continuous density $f$ at $x$ then $f(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\lim_{\eta \downarrow 0} \operatorname{Im} m(x + i\eta)$. The real part has the companion limit $\operatorname{Re} m(x + i\eta) \to \pi H_f(x) := \mathrm{PV}\int \frac{f(t)}{t - x}\,dt$ wherever $f$ is Hölder continuous, so the boundary value $\breve m(x) = \lim_{\eta\downarrow0} m(x + i\eta) = \pi H_f(x) + i\pi f(x)$ (Sokhotski-Plemelj). In particular two measures with the same Stieltjes transform on $\mathbb{C}^+$ coincide, and a sequence of probability measures converges weakly if and only if the Stieltjes transforms converge pointwise on $\mathbb{C}^+$ (to the transform of a probability measure).
mu a finite positive Borel measure on the real line
for the density statement: mu absolutely continuous with a density continuous at x; for the real-part statement: the density Hölder continuous near x

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Review the failure of perturbation theory and test a restricted version on a tree-like subgraph. Result: On the Bethe lattice a.c. spectrum is known (Klein; Aizenman-Warzel) because the self-consistent equation for the Green function has a stable solution; on Z^3 the corresponding equation is not closed. A known partial statement is that the disorder-averaged Green function has diffusive behaviour up to times lambda^{-2-delta} (Erdos-Salmhofer-Yau), which is the kinetic regime and does not reach the infinite-time statement. I tested the possibility of transferring the tree result through a spanning tree of Z^3: the operator restricted to a spanning tree is not the operator on Z^3, and removing the edges changes the spectrum non-perturbatively, so no transfer. No result; the problem is recorded as attempted with the explicit obstruction that the only tools proving a.c. spectrum are tree-specific. Obstruction: Absence of a closed self-consistency equation on Z^3; kinetic-regime results stop at finite times.

ATTEMPT RECORD, author-checked only, from the 2026-09-07 intake. Method: Try a fractional-moment (Aizenman-Molchanov) argument adapted to band matrices at fixed W in d = 2. Result: The fractional-moment method proves localisation when the expected s-th moment of the Green function E|G_{xy}(E + i eta)|^s decays exponentially in |x - y|; for band matrices at fixed W in d = 2 the required a priori bound is a decoupling of the moment across a band-width-sized block, which for the Anderson model comes from the rank-one structure of the diagonal disorder. Band matrices have no rank-one structure: the randomness at a site is a W^2-dimensional block, and the decoupling lemma degrades by a factor that grows with W^2, so the method proves localisation only for W <= W_0 small (large disorder regime), not for every fixed W. The conjectured localisation length exp(W^2) matches the expected scaling of the failure of the fractional-moment bound: the moment decays only after distances of order exp(cW^2), consistent with the conjecture but not proving it. A rigorous partial statement I can defend: for every fixed W there is a positive density of localised states at the spectral edges (Lifshitz-tail regime), by the standard edge-localisation argument, which does not touch the bulk. No bulk result. Obstruction: Fractional-moment decoupling loses a factor growing with W^2; no method reaches exp(W^2) localisation lengths.

Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent q = p/(p-1) (q = infinity when p = 1). For 1 < p < infinity the map g -> (f -> integral f g dmu) is an isometric isomorphism from L^q(mu) onto the dual space L^p(mu)^*, for ANY measure space. For p = 1 the same map from L^infinity(mu) onto L^1(mu)^* is an isometric isomorphism provided mu is sigma-finite (or, more generally, localizable); without such a hypothesis it can fail to be surjective. The dual of L^infinity is strictly larger than L^1 whenever L^infinity is infinite-dimensional: on ([0,1], Lebesgue) a Banach limit or a Hahn-Banach extension of the functional f -> lim_{x -> 0} f(x) from C[0,1] gives an element of (L^infinity)^* not represented by any L^1 function. So the duality chain (L^1)^* = L^infinity does NOT continue to (L^infinity)^* = L^1, and L^1 is not reflexive; L^p is reflexive exactly for 1 < p < infinity. [standard; e.g. Folland, Real Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 6.15]
1 <= p < infinity
for p = 1: mu sigma-finite (or localizable)
no hypothesis on mu for 1 < p < infinity

Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be SIGMA-FINITE positive measures on M. Then nu can be written as nu = nu_a + nu_s with nu_a absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu_a << mu) and nu_s mutually singular with mu (nu_s perp mu), and this decomposition is unique. Combined with the Radon-Nikodym theorem, nu_a has a density: there is an M-measurable f >= 0, unique up to mu-null sets, with nu_a(E) = integral_E f dmu for all E in M; f is in L^1(mu) exactly when nu_a is a finite measure. The statement extends to nu a signed or complex measure of finite total variation with mu sigma-finite. WHERE IT FAILS: (a) sigma-finiteness of nu is essential for existence of the decomposition. Take X = [0,1] with the Borel sets, mu = Lebesgue measure and nu = counting measure. If nu = nu_a + nu_s with nu_a << mu and nu_s perp mu, pick E with mu(E) = 0 and nu_s(X minus E) = 0. For any x outside E we get nu({x}) = nu_a({x}), and mu({x}) = 0 forces nu_a({x}) = 0, contradicting nu({x}) = 1. So X minus E is empty, i.e. E = X, contradicting mu(X) = 1 > 0. (b) sigma-finiteness of mu is essential for the DENSITY. With mu = counting measure on [0,1] and nu = Lebesgue measure one has nu << mu, yet no f satisfies nu(E) = integral_E f dmu (evaluating on singletons forces f = 0). The decomposition itself survives here (nu_s = 0), but the Radon-Nikodym half does not. (c) Uniqueness is uniqueness of the pair of measures; the density f is only mu-almost everywhere unique.
(X, M) is a measurable space
mu is sigma-finite (needed for the Radon-Nikodym density)
nu is sigma-finite (needed for existence of the decomposition); for signed or complex nu, finite total variation
absolute continuity and mutual singularity are with respect to the same sigma-algebra M

rows.body: Radon-Nikodym theorem: if mu and nu are sigma-finite measures on the same measurable space and nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu (mu-null sets are nu-null), then there is a nonnegative measurable density f, unique up to mu-null sets, with nu(A) equal to the integral of f over A against mu for every measurable A; f is the Radon-Nikodym derivative dnu/dmu. Sigma-finiteness cannot be dropped (Lebesgue measure against counting measure on R fails).
rows.title: Radon-Nikodym theorem

rows.body:
Let mu and nu be sigma-finite measures on a measurable space (X, Sigma) with nu absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu(A)=0 whenever mu(A)=0, written nu << mu). Then there exists a non-negative measurable function f = dnu/dmu, unique mu-almost-everywhere, such that nu(A) = integral over A of f dmu for every A in Sigma. f is the Radon-Nikodym derivative; the theorem is the measure-theoretic foundation of conditional expectation and of probability densities.
mu, nu sigma-finite measures
nu absolutely continuous w.r.t. mu
